results.title: Virtue environmentalism: towards a robustly social virtue epistemology | Synthese | Springer Nature Link
results.content: This paper aims to present a robustly social account of virtue epistemology, framed within the context of the epistemic social environment. To achieve this, it draws on key insights from feminist epistemology and vice epistemology, particularly the work of Johnson, Grasswick, and Kidd. It argues that we can socialize epistemic virtues by broadening our focus from individual epistemic goods to the wider variety of goods that improve our epistemic social environment. Moreover, it offers a new perspective on the ongoing debate concerning the relationship between epistemology and intellectual ethics. ### From Virtue Ethics to Virtue Epistemology. In many cases, even if papers do not explicitly address core themes of social epistemology—such as testimony, peer disagreement, or group knowledge—they often engage with classical epistemological issues from a social perspective, selecting cases and objections accordingly.Footnote 1 One consequence of this shift is that various epistemological positions and approaches have been compelled to reckon with the social turn, undergoing a process of socialization in different ways.

results.title: Socializing Virtue Epistemology | Episteme | Cambridge Core
results.content: In recent years, virtue epistemology has been criticized for its individualism. However, there is some confusion about what it means for virtue epistemology to be individualistic, and how it should be socialized in the face of this. We distinguish elements of theories of virtue that might give rise to different forms of individualism: “subject individualism,” “faculty/trait individualism,” and “value individualism.” Then we show what specific challenges these elements might pose for virtue reliabilism and responsibilism. We focus on two challenges: the epistemic value of other-regarding intellectual virtues, and the problem of “epistemic outsourcing.” In both cases, we identify and evaluate possible strategies for socializing these elements of virtue epistemology. Unfortunately, a general lack of convergence between the two has often led, on the one hand, to virtue epistemology reinforcing epistemic individualism (Kallestrup & Pritchard, Reference Kallestrup and Pritchard2012), and on the other, social epistemology focusing primarily on structural and institutional approaches at the cost of personal ones.
